[ORIGINAL USER REQUEST]
A consumer app has grown to millions of active free users but converts under 2% to its paid tier, and investor patience with the losses is ending. Past monetization tests backfired: aggressive paywalls spiked uninstalls, and intrusive ads damaged app-store ratings within weeks. Usage data shows several distinct user segments that get very different value from the product.

Design a monetization strategy that meaningfully increases revenue per user while protecting retention and ratings. Choose and justify the mix of subscription tiers, usage-based pricing, advertising, and partnerships; map offers to the identified user segments; and define the experiment plan and guardrail metrics that will catch churn damage before it compounds.
[END ORIGINAL REQUEST]

[PREVIOUS AGENT OUTPUT]
# Monetization Architecture: Pricing the Frontier, Not the Floor

*A working draft. Read the framing sections as propositions rather than conclusions — most of them are testable within a quarter, and I'd rather they be tested than approved.*

---

## 1. What the failed tests were actually telling us

Two data points are usually treated as evidence that "users won't pay." I'd suggest they're evidence of something narrower and more fixable.

- **The paywall spike in uninstalls** happened because the wall was placed in front of behavior users had already internalized as free. That isn't a pricing failure; it's a *retroactive tax* on habit. People don't churn over price — they churn over loss.
- **The ads damaging ratings** happened because attention was extracted from the core loop, indiscriminately, from every segment — including the users whose only real contribution is bringing other users in. The revenue was real. It was simply smaller than the acquisition cost it quietly destroyed. Which raises a question worth putting on the wall: *has anyone priced a tenth of a star?*

So the operating principle for everything below:

> **Never charge for what a user already has. Charge for what they're about to want, in the currency they actually hold.**

Users hold four currencies: **money, attention, social reach, and consent.** A sub-2% conversion rate isn't a monetization ceiling — it's what happens when you only ever ask for one of the four, at one price, on one step.

---

## 2. Segment map

The usage data reportedly shows distinct segments. I'd propose organizing them on two axes that matter more than demographics or feature affinity: **willingness to pay** and **willingness to be interrupted**. Sizes below are illustrative placeholders — substitute your clustering output, but keep the archetypes, since the offer logic follows from them.

| # | Segment | ~% of MAU | Behavioral signature | Currency they hold | Monetization posture |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Power / prosumer** | 3–5% | Deep sessions, advanced features, hits limits, often using a consumer app for semi-professional work | Money (high) | Under-monetized today. Ladder *up*, aggressively. |
| 2 | **Habitual light** | 20–25% | Daily or near-daily, shallow, narrow feature set, high friction sensitivity | Money (small, reliable) + attention | The uninstall spike lived here. Micro-price, never wall. |
| 3 | **Episodic high-intent** | 12–18% | Dormant, then intense bursts (a trip, a project, a season) | Money (burst) | Monthly subscription is structurally wrong for them. Passes and credits. |
| 4 | **Amplifiers** | 8–12% | Modest direct usage, outsized invites/shares/referral-attributed installs | Social reach | Monetize *indirectly*. Treat as protected. Zero ads, zero gates. |
| 5 | **Drifters & new** | 40–50% | Low frequency, unactivated, high churn hazard | Attention + consent | Activation first. Then low-load ads, commerce, partner-sponsored access. |
| 6 | **Latent teams / B2B pockets** | <1% of users, potentially 15–25% of upside | Multi-device, shared accounts, export-heavy, workday usage patterns | Money (much higher than consumer) | Highest ARPU per unit of effort in the whole plan. Find these first. |

Segment 6 is the one I'd look for hardest before anything else ships. Consumer apps with millions of users almost always have a few thousand people quietly running a business inside them, paying $10 for something they'd expense at $150. Worth a single afternoon with the export logs and workday-hour usage curves.

---

## 3. The revenue mix

Four instruments, deliberately layered so that each one *feeds* the next rather than competing with it.

### 3.1 Subscription: replace the cliff with a ladder

One tier at one price fits one willingness-to-pay. Four price points fit four.

| Tier | Price | Contents | Primary segment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Free** | $0 | Everything users have today, plus one or two *additions* (see note) | 4, 5 |
| **Lite** | $2.49/mo · $17.99/yr | Ad-free, annoyance removal, modest quota lift, one cosmetic/identity perk | 2 |
| **Pro** | $9.99/mo · $79/yr | Current paid tier, re-merchandised: unlimited core quota, advanced features, multi-device, priority | 1, 3 (converted) |
| **Max** | $24.99/mo · $199/yr | Pro + bundled usage credits, API/bulk export, early access, human support | 1, 6 |
| **Teams** | $13/seat/mo, 3 seat min | Shared workspace, admin, billing, SSO later | 6 |

Two design choices I'd defend if pushed:

**Free gets *better*, not worse.** Ship one genuinely new free capability in the same release as the ladder. It costs little and it changes the story from "they're taking things away" to "they built more, and some of it costs money." Store reviews are written about narratives, not feature matrices.

**Lite exists mostly to move Pro.** Its direct revenue is thin. Its job is to (a) capture the habitual segment that will never pay $10, (b) act as a price anchor that makes Pro read as *value* rather than *the price*, and (c) create a graceful landing spot for cancelling Pro subscribers who currently churn to zero. Expect 30–40% of Lite signups to be saved churn, not new revenue — and account for it honestly rather than counting it twice.

**Guard against cannibalization** by keeping Lite deliberately unattractive to power users: no quota expansion beyond modest, no advanced features, no exports. If Pro→Lite downgrade exceeds ~8% of the Pro base in a quarter, Lite is over-specified.

### 3.2 Usage-based: meter the frontier, never the habit

Metering works where marginal cost or marginal *intent* is high. It fails catastrophically where it touches the habit loop.

- **Credits** on expensive or burst actions only: generation, rendering, bulk export, storage, boosts, priority processing. Never on the two or three actions that constitute the daily habit.
- **Soft limits, not walls.** When a quota is reached, degrade — slower, queued, watermarked, lower resolution — with the paid path visible beside the free one. The previous test's hard block is precisely the mechanic that produced the uninstalls. A user who waits is retained; a user who is blocked writes a review.
- **Day pass $1.99 / week pass $5.99**, surfaced *only* at a detected intent moment, for Segment 3. Critically: **pass spend credits toward the first month of a subscription.** Episodic users who buy three passes in a year are subscription prospects you'd otherwise never see.
- **Top-ups over overages.** Never auto-bill a surprise. Surprise charges generate chargebacks, one-star reviews, and eventually regulatory attention.

### 3.3 Advertising: an opt-in and partner business, not a programmatic one

Ads aren't the problem; *undifferentiated interruption* was. I'd rebuild the ad business with four constraints:

1. **Rewarded and opt-in first.** "Watch 30s → 3 credits" or "→ unlock this feature today." Users choose to trade attention. Historically these carry near-zero rating damage because the user initiated the exchange, and they double as a paywall softener for people who genuinely can't pay.
2. **Native, low-load placements** confined to browse/discovery surfaces. Zero interstitials in the core loop. A hard session-level **ad load budget**, tuned per segment, treated as an explicitly priced variable.
3. **Exclusion lists, non-negotiable.** No ads for: users in their first N sessions, Amplifiers, anyone above a churn-risk threshold, anyone within 14 days of a rating prompt, all paying tiers.
4. **Sold, not remnant.** A small number of relevant sponsors at high CPM beats programmatic filler at low CPM — better creative, better brand safety, better ratings, fewer SDKs, less app bloat (which was probably half the rating damage last time — worth checking the crash and cold-start telemetry from that period).

And the mechanism that makes ads strategically coherent: **ad-free is Lite's headline benefit.** Every impression served to a habitual user is also a conversion argument. Ads that sell subscriptions are worth more than their CPM.

### 3.4 Partnerships: the revenue with no UX cost

The most underused lever in this situation, and the one I'd personally spend my time on.

- **Sponsored premium (B2B2C).** An employer, insurer, bank, telco, or retailer buys Pro for its members. You collect $4–7/user/month at scale with *zero* attention extracted and *positive* user sentiment. This is the single highest-leverage line item in the plan and requires no product risk at all.
- **Commerce and affiliate**, wherever user intent is already transactional. Often rating-*positive*, because it adds utility rather than subtracting attention.
- **Distribution bundles** — carrier and OEM preloads, bundled with other subscriptions. Lowers CAC and adds a revenue floor.
- **Gifting and peer payments** for Amplifiers: let them buy Pro for a friend, take 10–20%. Monetizes social reach in the currency they actually hold.
- **Aggregated, consented insight products** — panel-based, opt-in, never individual-level. Real money, real reputational exposure. I'd hold this until the core plan is working, and I'd only do it with an explicit consent surface a journalist could read without finding a story.

### 3.5 What the mix might produce

Illustrative, on 5M MAU, substituting your real elasticities:

| Line | Penetration | Net/unit | ARPU/MAU |
|---|---|---|---|
| Today (single tier) | 2.0% | $8.50 | **$0.17** |
| Lite | 4.0% | $2.10 | $0.084 |
| Pro | 2.2% | $8.50 | $0.187 |
| Max + Teams | 0.4% | $21.00 | $0.084 |
| Passes & credits | 3.0% of MAU/mo | $1.30 | $0.039 |
| Ads (eligible ~55% of MAU) | — | — | $0.150 |
| Commerce + partnerships | — | — | $0.110 |
| **Total** | | | **~$0.65** |

Roughly 3.5–4x ARPU, with under half of it coming from raw subscription conversion. Note what the model *doesn't* rely on: it doesn't need conversion to reach 6%. That's the point of the ladder — you diversify the ask instead of intensifying it.

---

## 4. Segment → offer mapping

| Segment | Primary ask | Secondary | Never do this |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Power / prosumer** | Max, at 2.5x current price, with credits bundled | Teams upsell, API | Don't cap them into Pro; you're leaving money there |
| **Habitual light** | Lite, in-context after 21+ days of use | Rewarded ads for occasional unlocks | Any hard gate on their daily action. This is where the last test died |
| **Episodic high-intent** | Day/week pass at the intent moment | Pass-to-subscription credit | Monthly-only pricing; annual pitch during a burst |
| **Amplifiers** | G

# Critique: "Monetization Architecture: Pricing the Frontier, Not the Floor"

## 1. Fatal, structural problem: the deliverable is incomplete

The output terminates mid-word ("**Amplifiers** | G") in the segment-offer table. As a result, **two of the four explicitly requested components are entirely missing**:

- the **experiment plan** (sequencing, holdouts, sample sizing, decision rules, rollout mechanics)
- the **guardrail metrics** that "catch churn damage before it compounds"

Given that the user's stated history is *two monetization tests that backfired*, the experiment and guardrail design was arguably the highest-value section of the brief. Everything shipped so far is the part the client could have gotten from any pricing consultant; the missing part is the part they actually got burned on. This alone requires a rewrite, not a patch.

## 2. Errors and unsupported numbers in the revenue model

**App-store fee assumption is wrong or unstated.** Pro at $9.99 with "$8.50 net" implies a ~15% take rate. Apple/Google charge 30% on first-year subscriptions (15% thereafter), and the 15% Small Business Program caps at $1M annual proceeds — irrelevant for a company with millions of MAU and investor scale. Lite at $2.49 nets ~$1.74 in year one, not $2.10. Correcting fees knocks roughly 15–20% off the entire subscription column. This is a first-order arithmetic error in the headline claim.

**Internal contradiction on the conversion narrative.** The model's paid penetration sums to 4.0% + 2.2% + 0.4% = **6.6%**, yet the closing line says "it doesn't need conversion to reach 6%. That's the point of the ladder." The model does exactly what it claims not to require. Either the framing or the numbers must change.

**Pro penetration is assumed to rise (2.0% → 2.2%) while a cheaper adjacent tier is introduced.** The document itself concedes 30–40% of Lite is cannibalized/saved churn. Assuming simultaneous Pro *growth* under a Lite launch is an optimistic assumption presented as arithmetic. A downside case (Pro falls to 1.6%) is not shown.

**Ads at $0.15/MAU and commerce+partnerships at $0.11/MAU carry 40% of the incremental ARPU with zero derivation.** These are the two least-validated lines and the two hardest to build, and they are asserted. Meanwhile the ad estimate is internally inconsistent with the aggressive exclusion lists (new users, Amplifiers, churn-risk cohort, all payers, pre-rating-prompt windows) — those exclusions plausibly remove half the eligible impressions, and no reconciliation is offered.

**No cost side, and therefore no answer to the actual business problem.** The brief says *investor patience with the losses is ending*. The plan produces ~$39M/yr vs ~$10M/yr today on 5M MAU — but never states burn, CAC, gross margin, infra cost per free user, or months to breakeven. Without that bridge, the client cannot tell an investor whether this plan closes the gap or gets a third of the way there. Cost-side levers (infra cost per unactivated free user, paid-acquisition pullback, support automation) are absent entirely.

## 3. Segmentation weaknesses

- **Segment sizes sum to 84–111%** — the low end doesn't reach 100%, which means the taxonomy is either incomplete or the ranges are decorative.
- **The segments are not mutually exclusive.** A Power user can also be an Amplifier; an Episodic user can sit inside a Latent Team. Since the offer logic is per-segment and includes hard exclusions ("Amplifiers: zero ads, zero gates"), the plan *requires* a precedence hierarchy for conflicting assignments. None is given, and this is exactly the kind of gap that produces an accidental ad served to a top referrer.
- **Several targeting rules depend on models that may not exist**: a churn-risk score, an intent-moment detector for pass surfacing, referral attribution good enough to identify Amplifiers. Each is a prerequisite with real build time. They are treated as available primitives.
- **Segment 6 (Teams/B2B) is credited with "15–25% of upside" on no evidence**, and Teams delivery (shared workspace, admin, billing, SSO) is a substantial engineering program hidden behind a single table row. The right move — concierge/manual-invoice validation with 20 hand-identified accounts before building anything — is not proposed.

## 4. Logical inconsistencies in the design principles

**The core principle is violated by the core plan.** "Never charge for what a user already has" and "Free gets *better*, not worse" sit directly beside a plan to introduce ads to free users and to make ad-free the headline Lite benefit. Perceived removal is removal; this is precisely the mechanic that produced the last rating collapse. The document needs an explicit reconciliation — e.g., ads confined to *newly built* surfaces only, or ad exposure applied only to cohorts acquired after launch, with legacy cohorts grandfathered. Absent that, the plan repeats the mistake it opens by diagnosing.

**"Ads that sell subscriptions"** creates a structural incentive to degrade the free experience toward the conversion-maximizing level. Without a hard-coded, independently owned ad-load ceiling and a rating-linked circuit breaker, this incentive wins over time. The plan names an "ad load budget" but assigns no owner, no ceiling, and no escalation rule.

**Soft-degradation is asserted as safe** ("a user who waits is retained; a user who is blocked writes a review"). Plausible, but it is a hypothesis, and queuing/watermarking a habitual action is still a loss event. It should be tested as such, not stated as a fact.

## 5. Missing content a monetization plan of this scope requires

- **Involuntary churn / payment recovery.** Typically 20–40% of subscription churn and the cheapest revenue in the building. Completely absent. This should be week-one work, ahead of any pricing change.
- **Grandfathering and price-change communication policy** for existing paid users, including EU/UK consent requirements for subscription price increases and Apple's price-increase consent flow. Raising Power users to "2.5x current price" without addressing existing-subscriber treatment is a rating incident waiting to happen.
- **Willingness-to-pay research method.** Prices are asserted ($2.49, $9.99, $24.99, $13/seat) with no Van Westendorp / conjoint / discrete-choice / historical-elasticity basis.
- **Regional/PPP pricing.** Millions of MAU in a consumer app implies large low-ARPU geographies where $9.99 is unsellable and where ad monetization is the only viable path. No geographic differentiation at all.

# Monetization Architecture: Pricing the Frontier, Not the Floor

*A working draft. Read the framing sections as propositions rather than conclusions — most of them are testable within a quarter, and I'd rather they be tested than approved.*

---

## 1. What the failed tests were actually telling us

Two data points are usually treated as evidence that "users won't pay." I'd suggest they're evidence of something narrower and more fixable.

- **The paywall spike in uninstalls** happened because the wall was placed in front of behavior users had already internalized as free. That isn't a pricing failure; it's a *retroactive tax* on habit. People don't churn over price — they churn over loss.
- **The ads damaging ratings** happened because attention was extracted from the core loop, indiscriminately, from every segment — including the users whose only real contribution is bringing other users in. The revenue was real. It was simply smaller than the acquisition cost it quietly destroyed. Which raises a question worth putting on the wall: *has anyone priced a tenth of a star?*

So the operating principle for everything below:

> **Never charge for what a user already has. Charge for what they're about to want, in the currency they actually hold.**

Users hold four currencies: **money, attention, social reach, and consent.** A sub-2% conversion rate isn't a monetization ceiling — it's what happens when you only ever ask for one of the four, at one price, on one step.

---

## 2. Segment map

The usage data reportedly shows distinct segments. I'd propose organizing them on two axes that matter more than demographics or feature affinity: **willingness to pay** and **willingness to be interrupted**. Sizes below are illustrative placeholders — substitute your clustering output, but keep the archetypes, since the offer logic follows from them.

| # | Segment | ~% of MAU | Behavioral signature | Currency they hold | Monetization posture |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Power / prosumer** | 3–5% | Deep sessions, advanced features, hits limits, often using a consumer app for semi-professional work | Money (high) | Under-monetized today. Ladder *up*, aggressively. |
| 2 | **Habitual light** | 20–25% | Daily or near-daily, shallow, narrow feature set, high friction sensitivity | Money (small, reliable) + attention | The uninstall spike lived here. Micro-price, never wall. |
| 3 | **Episodic high-intent** | 12–18% | Dormant, then intense bursts (a trip, a project, a season) | Money (burst) | Monthly subscription is structurally wrong for them. Passes and credits. |
| 4 | **Amplifiers** | 8–12% | Modest direct usage, outsized invites/shares/referral-attributed installs | Social reach | Monetize *indirectly*. Treat as protected. Zero ads, zero gates. |
| 5 | **Drifters & new** | 40–50% | Low frequency, unactivated, high churn hazard | Attention + consent | Activation first. Then low-load ads, commerce, partner-sponsored access. |
| 6 | **Latent teams / B2B pockets** | <1% of users, potentially 15–25% of upside | Multi-device, shared accounts, export-heavy, workday usage patterns | Money (much higher than consumer) | Highest ARPU per unit of effort in the whole plan. Find these first. |

Segment 6 is the one I'd look for hardest before anything else ships. Consumer apps with millions of users almost always have a few thousand people quietly running a business inside them, paying $10 for something they'd expense at $150. Worth a single afternoon with the export logs and workday-hour usage curves.

---

## 3. The revenue mix

Four instruments, deliberately layered so that each one *feeds* the next rather than competing with it.

### 3.1 Subscription: replace the cliff with a ladder

One tier at one price fits one willingness-to-pay. Four price points fit four.

| Tier | Price | Contents | Primary segment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Free** | $0 | Everything users have today, plus one or two *additions* (see note) | 4, 5 |
| **Lite** | $2.49/mo · $17.99/yr | Ad-free, annoyance removal, modest quota lift, one cosmetic/identity perk | 2 |
| **Pro** | $9.99/mo · $79/yr | Current paid tier, re-merchandised: unlimited core quota, advanced features, multi-device, priority | 1, 3 (converted) |
| **Max** | $24.99/mo · $199/yr | Pro + bundled usage credits, API/bulk export, early access, human support | 1, 6 |
| **Teams** | $13/seat/mo, 3 seat min | Shared workspace, admin, billing, SSO later | 6 |

Two design choices I'd defend if pushed:

**Free gets *better*, not worse.** Ship one genuinely new free capability in the same release as the ladder. It costs little and it changes the story from "they're taking things away" to "they built more, and some of it costs money." Store reviews are written about narratives, not feature matrices.

**Lite exists mostly to move Pro.** Its direct revenue is thin. Its job is to (a) capture the habitual segment that will never pay $10, (b) act as a price anchor that makes Pro read as *value* rather than *the price*, and (c) create a graceful landing spot for cancelling Pro subscribers who currently churn to zero. Expect 30–40% of Lite signups to be saved churn, not new revenue — and account for it honestly rather than counting it twice.

**Guard against cannibalization** by keeping Lite deliberately unattractive to power users: no quota expansion beyond modest, no advanced features, no exports. If Pro→Lite downgrade exceeds ~8% of the Pro base in a quarter, Lite is over-specified.

### 3.2 Usage-based: meter the frontier, never the habit

Metering works where marginal cost or marginal *intent* is high. It fails catastrophically where it touches the habit loop.

- **Credits** on expensive or burst actions only: generation, rendering, bulk export, storage, boosts, priority processing. Never on the two or three actions that constitute the daily habit.
- **Soft limits, not walls.** When a quota is reached, degrade — slower, queued, watermarked, lower resolution — with the paid path visible beside the free one. The previous test's hard block is precisely the mechanic that produced the uninstalls. A user who waits is retained; a user who is blocked writes a review.
- **Day pass $1.99 / week pass $5.99**, surfaced *only* at a detected intent moment, for Segment 3. Critically: **pass spend credits toward the first month of a subscription.** Episodic users who buy three passes in a year are subscription prospects you'd otherwise never see.
- **Top-ups over overages.** Never auto-bill a surprise. Surprise charges generate chargebacks, one-star reviews, and eventually regulatory attention.

### 3.3 Advertising: an opt-in and partner business, not a programmatic one

Ads aren't the problem; *undifferentiated interruption* was. I'd rebuild the ad business with four constraints:

1. **Rewarded and opt-in first.** "Watch 30s → 3 credits" or "→ unlock this feature today." Users choose to trade attention. Historically these carry near-zero rating damage because the user initiated the exchange, and they double as a paywall softener for people who genuinely can't pay.
2. **Native, low-load placements** confined to browse/discovery surfaces. Zero interstitials in the core loop. A hard session-level **ad load budget**, tuned per segment, treated as an explicitly priced variable.
3. **Exclusion lists, non-negotiable.** No ads for: users in their first N sessions, Amplifiers, anyone above a churn-risk threshold, anyone within 14 days of a rating prompt, all paying tiers.
4. **Sold, not remnant.** A small number of relevant sponsors at high CPM beats programmatic filler at low CPM — better creative, better brand safety, better ratings, fewer SDKs, less app bloat (which was probably half the rating damage last time — worth checking the crash and cold-start telemetry from that period).

And the mechanism that makes ads strategically coherent: **ad-free is Lite's headline benefit.** Every impression served to a habitual user is also a conversion argument. Ads that sell subscriptions are worth more than their CPM.

### 3.4 Partnerships: the revenue with no UX cost

The most underused lever in this situation, and the one I'd personally spend my time on.

- **Sponsored premium (B2B2C).** An employer, insurer, bank, telco, or retailer buys Pro for its members. You collect $4–7/user/month at scale with *zero* attention extracted and *positive* user sentiment. This is the single highest-leverage line item in the plan and requires no product risk at all.
- **Commerce and affiliate**, wherever user intent is already transactional. Often rating-*positive*, because it adds utility rather than subtracting attention.
- **Distribution bundles** — carrier and OEM preloads, bundled with other subscriptions. Lowers CAC and adds a revenue floor.
- **Gifting and peer payments** for Amplifiers: let them buy Pro for a friend, take 10–20%. Monetizes social reach in the currency they actually hold.
- **Aggregated, consented insight products** — panel-based, opt-in, never individual-level. Real money, real reputational exposure. I'd hold this until the core plan is working, and I'd only do it with an explicit consent surface a journalist could read without finding a story.

### 3.5 What the mix might produce

Illustrative, on 5M MAU, substituting your real elasticities:

| Line | Penetration | Net/unit | ARPU/MAU |
|---|---|---|---|
| Today (single tier) | 2.0% | $8.50 | **$0.17** |
| Lite | 4.0% | $2.10 | $0.084 |
| Pro | 2.2% | $8.50 | $0.187 |
| Max + Teams | 0.4% | $21.00 | $0.084 |
| Passes & credits | 3.0% of MAU/mo | $1.30 | $0.039 |
| Ads (eligible ~55% of MAU) | — | — | $0.150 |
| Commerce + partnerships | — | — | $0.110 |
| **Total** | | | **~$0.65** |

Roughly 3.5–4x ARPU, with under half of it coming from raw subscription conversion. Note what the model *doesn't* rely on: it doesn't need conversion to reach 6%. That's the point of the ladder — you diversify the ask instead of intensifying it.

---

## 4. Segment → offer mapping

| Segment | Primary ask | Secondary | Never do this |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Power / prosumer** | Max, at 2.5x current price, with credits bundled | Teams upsell, API | Don't cap them into Pro; you're leaving money there |
| **Habitual light** | Lite, in-context after 21+ days of use | Rewarded ads for occasional unlocks | Any hard gate on their daily action. This is where the last test died |
| **Episodic high-intent** | Day/week pass at the intent moment | Pass-to-subscription credit | Monthly-only pricing; annual pitch during a burst |
